Abraham Booth
AY-bruh-ham BOOTH
proper noun
Hebrew given name Abraham, “father of a multitude”; the surname Booth, from the Old Norse búð, “a dwelling or shelter.”

📖 Biblical Definition

Abraham Booth (1734–1806) was an eighteenth-century Particular Baptist pastor who served the congregation at Prescot Street, London, for nearly forty years. Reared in humble circumstances and largely self-taught, Booth was for a season inclined to the doctrine of general redemption, but upon deeper searching of the Scriptures he was brought to embrace the doctrines of sovereign grace, and out of that conviction he wrote his enduring work, The Reign of Grace. In it he traces the dominion of grace from its eternal source in election, through the cross of Christ, into the regeneration, justification, adoption, sanctification, and final perseverance of the saints, showing at every step that grace reigns through righteousness unto eternal life and that salvation from first to last is the free gift of God. Booth set grace in deliberate contrast to all schemes of human merit, insisting that the believer owes everything to the unmerited favor of the LORD. He was esteemed among his brethren as a man of integrity, doctrinal soundness, and pastoral diligence, and he contended earnestly against errors that would dishonor free grace. His writings, marked by clarity and scriptural fullness, ministered to his own generation and to many since, exalting the God who saves to the praise of the glory of His grace and abasing the pride of man, who has nothing he did not first receive.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

An eighteenth-century Particular Baptist pastor of London, author of The Reign of Grace.

expand to see more

ABRAHAM BOOTH, English Particular Baptist pastor (1734–1806), minister at Prescot Street, London, for nearly forty years.

Largely self-taught, he turned from general redemption to the doctrines of sovereign grace.

Author of The Reign of Grace, tracing grace from election to final perseverance.

He set free grace against every scheme of human merit (Rom 5:21).

Esteemed among his brethren for integrity, sound doctrine, and pastoral diligence.

📖 Key Scripture

Rom 5:21 — "That as sin hath reigned unto death, even so might grace reign through righteousness unto eternal life by Jesus Christ our Lord."

Eph 2:8 — "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:"

Tit 2:11 — "For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men,"

2Co 12:9 — "And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Booth’s doctrine of reigning grace is recovered against an age that hollows the word “grace” into mere niceness or general tolerance.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Yet the word at the heart of Booth’s labor is constantly counterfeited. The world borrows “grace” to mean a vague kindliness, an easy tolerance, or a pardon that costs nothing and changes nothing. Booth’s Reign of Grace recovers the biblical meaning: unmerited favor that reigns through righteousness, purchased by the blood of Christ and applied sovereignly to the elect, transforming as well as forgiving.

The lesson to recover is that grace is a reigning power, not a passive sentiment—it dethrones sin, justifies the guilty, and carries the saint to glory. Booth set grace against all merit precisely so that God should have all the praise. Where the present age cheapens grace into mere leniency, Booth restores it as the costly, conquering favor of God that saves from first to last.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Abraham means “father of a multitude”; Booth denotes a shelter or dwelling.

expand to see more

Abraham — from Hebrew Abraham, “father of a multitude.”

Booth, from Old Norse búð, “a temporary dwelling or shelter.”

Grace, from the Latin gratia, rendering the Greek charis, “unmerited favor.”

Reign, from the Latin regnare, “to rule as king,” as grace reigns through righteousness (Rom 5:21).

Redemption, from the Latin redimere, “to buy back,” the price Booth saw fixed by sovereign grace.

Usage

"Abraham Booth traced the reign of grace from election to glory."

"Once inclined to general redemption, Abraham Booth came to confess sovereign grace."

"For nearly forty years Abraham Booth shepherded the Prescot Street congregation."
